sections.text:
Humanoid motion-tracking policies can reproduce diverse behaviors, yet connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence remains challenging. Interpolation connects boundary poses without considering whether their relative position, heading, and timing provide suitable conditions for a transition.

A generative motion prior can produce richer motion, but poorly arranged boundaries may cause it to generate excessive locomotion, turning, or another unintended action. We present Spatio-Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a framework for connecting independently acquired humanoid motions through a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot process.

STAMP uses human motion space to draw on rich motion priors and reuse transition knowledge across robot embodiments. Its key component is a learned alignment model that determines the boundary conditions for motion inbetweening.

Given the two motions retargeted to a human rig, the alignment model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion. A human motion prior generates the transition under the selected alignment. The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot and used as a reference to train a motion-tracking policy.

We evaluate the tracking success of the generated transitions on Unitree~G1 and~ROBOTIS K1.Physical robot demonstrations further show that STAMP connects independently acquired motions into long-horizon sequences. Project page: https://childtoy.github.io/STAMP-project

summary.en: The paper presents STAMP, which connects independently acquired humanoid motions through a robot-to-human-to-robot process. After retargeting motions to a human rig, a learned alignment model selects candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion; a human motion prior then generates the transition. The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot as a reference for training a motion-tracking policy. The authors evaluate transition-tracking success on Unitree G1 and ROBOTIS K1, and use physical robot demonstrations to show connections in long-horizon sequences.
summary.zh: 论文提出 STAMP，通过“机器人到人再到机器人”的流程连接独立获取的人形机器人动作。它先将动作映射到人体骨架，再由学习到的对齐模型为后续动作筛选位置、朝向和过渡时长，并用人体动作先验生成衔接动作；完成序列随后重映射到机器人，用作训练动作跟踪策略的参考。作者在 Unitree G1 和 ROBOTIS K1 上评估生成过渡的跟踪成功情况，并通过实体机器人演示展示其连接动作、形成长时序列的能力。

sections.text:
Reliable robotic manipulation in field-deployed settings requires more than executing a capable controller. As the execution conditions change, the system must decide, online and on the robot side, which control source should hold authority.

Human teleoperation adapts readily to contact-rich and semantically ambiguous situations but depends on a stable communication link. Local autonomy is executed without continuous human intervention, but may fail under semantic ambiguity, long-horizon drift, and unforeseen contingencies. These two control sources exhibit complementary reliability profiles.

We formulate this complementarity as a control authority routing problem and present Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation (TEAR), an edge-deployable framework that allocates authority between human teleoperation and local autonomy.

TEAR arbitrates on the robot side using network-state evidence, which governs the usability of teleoperation, and task-semantic evidence, which reflects whether autonomous execution remains consistent with the current task.

A lightweight temporal arbitrator observes both forms of evidence together with robot state and current authority to time authority transfers.

Across simulated and real-world trials under dynamic network conditions, TEAR achieves task success rates close to pure teleoperation while limiting teleoperation to 19.8-27.4% of control steps and improves success by 30-40% over autonomy-only execution in our settings.

These results demonstrate the potential of complementary authority routing to sustain successful manipulation with substantially reduced dependence on continuous human control.

summary.en: The paper presents TEAR, an edge-deployable framework that routes control authority between human teleoperation and local autonomy. It uses network-state evidence to assess teleoperation usability and task-semantic evidence to assess whether autonomous execution remains aligned with the task. A temporal arbitrator also considers robot state and current authority when timing transfers. In simulated and real-world trials under dynamic network conditions, the authors report task success close to pure teleoperation while using teleoperation for 19.8–27.4% of control steps, and 30–40% higher success than autonomy-only execution in their settings.
summary.zh: 论文提出 TEAR，一种可部署于机器人端的框架，用于在人类远程操作与本地自主控制之间分配控制权。系统结合网络状态证据和任务语义证据，并由轻量级时间仲裁器参考机器人状态及当前控制权，决定何时转移控制。在动态网络条件下的仿真和真实场景试验中，作者报告其任务成功率接近纯远程操作，同时将远程操作限制在 19.8%–27.4% 的控制步骤；在所测试设置中，其成功率比仅自主控制高 30%–40%。

sections.text:
World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models.

A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations.

In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step.

Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better.

Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs.

It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

summary.en: The paper introduces FRED, which uses self-distillation to improve future video representations for World Action Models. It predicts representations from noise in a single denoising step, using representations from ground-truth future observations as targets, and conditions the video model on historical observations for temporal context. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, the authors report that FRED outperforms competing WAMs, with particularly large gains on long-horizon and zero-shot out-of-domain tasks. On tasks absent from robot training data and shown only in human videos, it reaches 50.0% success versus 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
summary.zh: 论文提出 FRED，通过自蒸馏提升世界动作模型从噪声中一次去噪得到的未来视频表征质量。训练时，模型以真实未来观测提取的表征为目标预测未来表征，并结合历史观测提供时间上下文。作者报告，FRED 在多种真实世界操作场景中持续优于对比模型，在长时序及零样本环境泛化任务中提升尤其明显；在人类视频展示而未出现在机器人训练数据中的任务上，成功率为 50.0%，对比模型最佳为 19.4%。

sections.text:
This paper presents TRACE, a traversability-aware reactive navigation framework designed for the autonomous operation of ground robots in unstructured forest environments.

Unlike traditional approaches, TRACE leverages VLM-based confidence maps from positive and negative natural-language prompt sets and combines them through evidential fusion to produce a dense traversability map that prioritizes the terrain based on signs of previously traversed paths.

Traversability-annotated points are then extracted and used to derive the left and right boundaries of the traversable path via percentile binning followed by spline or regularized polynomial fitting.

These boundaries are then incorporated as soft barrier constraints within an NMPC formulation, enabling safe and adaptive path following in complex natural environments. Rigorous experimental trials carried out in real-life forest environments demonstrate TRACE ability for smooth navigation in cluttered, deformable, and visually ambiguous terrains.

summary.en: The paper presents TRACE, a reactive navigation framework for ground robots in unstructured forest environments. It fuses visual-language-model confidence maps generated from positive and negative natural-language prompts into a dense traversability map that emphasizes signs of prior passage. Extracted points are used to fit path boundaries, which become soft barrier constraints in a nonlinear model predictive controller. The authors report real-world forest trials showing smooth navigation on cluttered, deformable, and visually ambiguous terrain.
summary.zh: 论文提出面向非结构化森林环境地面机器人的 TRACE 反应式导航框架。方法融合视觉语言模型依据正、负自然语言提示生成的置信图，形成强调既有通行迹象的稠密可通行性地图；再提取标注点并拟合路径左右边界，将其作为软障碍约束纳入非线性模型预测控制。作者称，真实森林环境中的实验表明，该方法能在杂乱、易变形且视觉模糊的地形中平稳导航。

items.title: TRACE: Traversability-aware Reactive Navigation via VLM-driven Adaptive Constraints Estimation

sections.text:
End-to-end control policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) have emerged as an alternative to conventional surgical robotic control approaches, with recent studies exploring state-based policies trained on privileged state observations.

However, such approaches rely on precise physical states that are difficult to obtain reliably in surgical environments.

Vision-based RL provides an alternative by learning manipulation policies directly from RGB observations, avoiding explicit state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines while enabling policies to acquire task-relevant visual representations.

Nevertheless, obtaining vision-based policies via pure RL methods for surgical manipulation remains challenging. Thus, imitation learning (IL) becomes another solution, yet it requires a large number of expert demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain in minimally invasive surgery.

In this work, we propose a framework for state-to-vision policy distillation in laparoscopic robotic manipulation.

Specifically, a state-based policy with privileged observations is employed as the teacher, and a vision-based policy learns from RGB observations and robot proprioceptive information, which requires less expert demonstrations than IL and introduces superior performance than RL methods.

We conduct extensive experiments on various surgical manipulation tasks in the simulated environment.

Experimental results show that, in the context of laparoscopic robotic manipulation, training vision-based policies with general-purpose RL methods is challenging, whereas our proposed state-to-vision policy distillation leads to more consistent and stable performance across tasks.

summary.en: The paper proposes state-to-vision policy distillation for laparoscopic robotic manipulation. A teacher policy uses privileged state observations, while a vision policy learns from RGB images and robot proprioception. The authors describe pure reinforcement learning for vision-based surgical manipulation as challenging and imitation learning as dependent on many difficult-to-obtain expert demonstrations. In simulated surgical manipulation tasks, their experiments find that the proposed distillation approach produces more consistent and stable performance across tasks than general-purpose reinforcement learning methods.
summary.zh: 论文研究腹腔镜机器人操作中的状态到视觉策略蒸馏：以使用特权状态观测的状态策略为教师，让视觉策略依据 RGB 图像和机器人本体感觉信息学习。作者指出，纯强化学习训练视觉策略较困难，而模仿学习需要难以获取的大量专家示范。该框架旨在减少对专家示范的需求。多种手术操作任务的仿真实验显示，与通用强化学习方法相比，所提蒸馏方法在不同任务上的表现更一致、更稳定。

items.title: Revisiting Distribution Matching for State-to-Vision Policy Distillation in Laparoscopic Robotic Manipulation

sections.text:
Language-conditioned humanoid motion generation enables users to create and refine robot movements through natural language. The central challenge is to connect an underspecified request to concrete motion structure that can subsequently be revised relative to an accepted reference.

We present TRACE, a generation and editing framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid robot built around typed, measurable kinematic quantities. Our insight is to ground generation conditions in paired training motions and editing goals in the current motion.

A language model learns to predict support, root, and hand events from motion-derived supervision; their time-aligned encodings complement the original text in a diffusion generator. Gravity-referenced states and trajectory--contact objectives improve kinematic consistency. For editing, typed requests define body--time scopes and source-relative goals.

A separate reference-conditioned diffusion editor uses these goals and revised events to realize changes, while sampling-time projection preserves protected state coordinates. Quantitative evaluation and human assessment show improved semantic alignment and motion quality over the compared methods.

Multi-turn editing evaluations demonstrate more reliable execution of successive relative requests under shared preservation constraints. Code is available at https://github.com/Multimodal-Perception-Action/TRACE.

summary.en: The paper presents TRACE, a motion generation and editing framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid. It uses measurable kinematic quantities, predicting support, root, and hand events from motion-derived supervision and adding time-aligned encodings to a diffusion generator. For editing, typed language requests specify body-time scopes and goals relative to the current motion; a reference-conditioned editor applies changes while projection preserves protected coordinates. Quantitative and human evaluations report better semantic alignment and motion quality than compared methods, and more reliable execution of successive relative requests.
summary.zh: 论文提出面向 Unitree G1 人形机器人的 TRACE 动作生成与编辑框架，以可测量的运动学量连接语言指令和动作结构。模型从动作监督中预测支撑、根部及手部事件，并将其时间对齐编码用于扩散生成；编辑时，类型化请求指定身体部位、时间范围和相对当前动作的目标，参考条件编辑器据此实现修改，并通过采样时投影保护指定状态坐标。定量评估和人工评价显示，相较对比方法，其语义对齐和动作质量有所提升；多轮评估显示连续相对请求执行更可靠。

sections.text:
Autonomous robots are moving rapidly from research labs into everyday life - on roads, in the air, in warehouses, and in space. Robot autonomy is no longer solely an academic pursuit, but a collection of mature, field-tested methods and tools that practitioners rely on in real-world deployments.

This book offers a clear, unified introduction to the methods that make this possible. Built on decades of teaching at Stanford, the text develops the core elements of modern autonomy stacks within a single conceptual framework, bridging classical robotics and modern physical AI.

Every major topic is paired with hands-on Jupyter notebooks and implementation-driven exercises, so readers build practical intuition alongside theoretical understanding. The result is a principled, accessible, and deployment-aware foundation for anyone seeking to design, analyze, or contribute to the next generation of autonomous systems.

This is a comprehensive resource for students, engineers, and researchers entering one of today's fastest-growing fields.

summary.en: This book offers a unified introduction to methods used in modern robot autonomy, connecting classical robotics with physical AI in a single conceptual framework. Drawing on decades of teaching, it is intended for students, engineers, and researchers entering the field. Major topics are accompanied by hands-on Jupyter notebooks and implementation-oriented exercises, pairing theoretical material with practical work. The abstract describes the book as an accessible, deployment-aware foundation for readers seeking to design, analyze, or contribute to autonomous systems.
summary.zh: 这本书介绍机器人自主系统的核心方法，并将经典机器人学与现代物理人工智能纳入统一的概念框架。内容基于作者数十年的教学，面向希望设计、分析或参与自主系统工作的学生、工程师和研究人员。书中主要主题配有 Jupyter 笔记本和以实现为导向的练习，旨在帮助读者在学习理论的同时建立实践理解。摘要将其定位为面向现实部署的入门基础资源。

Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success.

We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success.

To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.

items.title: Do VLAs Really Follow Instructions? Diagnosing How-Level Instruction Following in Vision-Language-Action Models

While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have leveraged internet-scale pretraining and task-specific finetuning to achieve strong performance on long-horizon tasks, they often struggle with non-Markovian tasks that require memory.

Existing approaches to memory typically involve additional Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) for long-term memory management, introducing a memory bottleneck and a fractured training pipeline.

Conditioning on multiple historical frames can provide the VLA with access to more descriptive features of past scenes, but can degrade performance if frames are chosen at arbitrary, fixed intervals. To address these limitations, we present UniMem, a framework that unifies high-level visual and textual memory and low-level control under one backbone.

UniMem employs an event classifier to initiate textual and visual memory updates, a keyframe encoder for dense visual memory, and a keyframe caching technique to minimize overhead during policy rollouts.

We evaluate UniMem across five simulation and four hardware tasks targeting sequential and spatial memory, demonstrating that our unified, single-model system outperforms fixed-interval image sampling baselines (93.4% vs. 68.2%) in simulation and hierarchical VLM-VLA baselines (80.0% vs. 43.5%) in hardware, while offering faster inference and a simple training pipeline for easy adoption.

Project website: https://losterberg3.github.io/unimem-vla/

items.title: UniMem: Unifying Visual and Textual Memory in VLAs for Non-Markovian Tasks

This paper presents a demonstration-based robotic feeding framework that integrates human demonstration, Dynamic Movement Primitive-based motion planning, vision-based scene perception, and robot control.

A human operator first demonstrates the scooping and feeding motions while the position and Euler-angle orientation of the spoon are recorded using a motion-capture system. The recorded trajectory is segmented into scooping and feeding motions, which are encoded using separate Dynamic Movement Primitives.

Before task execution, an RGB-D camera estimates the participant's mouth position, while two AprilTags are used for robot-frame registration and tray localization. The detected tray pose is used to position the scooping motion, whereas the detected mouth position defines the positional goal of the feeding motion.

The approach, scooping, and feeding trajectories are then executed sequentially by a Kinova Gen3 manipulator through a ROS~2-based framework. A real-world experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the integrated pipeline and shows that the learned spoon motions can be reproduced within the detected experimental scene.

items.title: Demonstration-Based Robotic Feeding Using Dynamic Movement Primitives

sections.text:
Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require $360^\circ$ perception to react to surrounding hazards.

While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation.

We present RangeNav, a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images.

We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird's-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning.

In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively.

Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced. Project website: https://rangenav.github.io/.

summary.en: The paper presents RangeNav, a compact LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data, using anisotropic convolutions and circular padding. Its navigation-aligned pretraining combines range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird’s-eye-view prediction; the encoder is then frozen for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision raises average success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments. The authors also report zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W, without quantitative deployment results in the abstract.
summary.zh: 论文提出RangeNav，一种完全使用合成数据预训练的紧凑型激光雷达距离图编码器，采用各向异性卷积和循环填充处理距离图的长宽比与方位接缝。其预训练目标结合距离重建、语义分割和鸟瞰图预测，随后冻结编码器进行策略学习。仿真中，相比仅用重建的基线，加入语义和鸟瞰图监督后，程序生成训练环境与分布外真实感测试环境的成功率平均分别提高32.03和23.73个百分点。作者还报告了Unitree B2-W四足机器人上的零样本真实部署表现；论文未提供该部署的量化结果。

sections.text:
Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages.

However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort.

Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts.

To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions.

Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control.

Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.

summary.en: The paper introduces Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which allocates optimization effort using keyframes and key body parts. A vision-language model selects motion signals and body parts; signal changes identify keyframes, which receive more solver iterations, while selected parts receive higher interaction weights. Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) refines contact positions with an approximate object-wrench model while retaining selected surface directions. sections.text:
Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy.

However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes.

To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments.

Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation.

Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects.

Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.

summary.en: The paper proposes OASIS for online mapping, open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. It represents scenes with sparse semantic anchor nodes that combine descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Compact memory, on-demand evidence extraction, and hierarchical retrieval are intended to reduce redundant storage and improve retrieval reliability. OASIS reuses transient observations gathered during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in simulation and real-world environments, covering standard retrieval benchmarks and static and dynamic navigation tasks, demonstrate complex retrieval and navigation, as well as relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.

Human manipulation videos provide rich motion and interaction cues for acquiring robot skills without robot demonstrations. Video generation models synthesize such demonstrations from an initial scene image and task instruction, avoiding the need to record demonstrations for each task.

However, the recovered motion captures only one scene-specific realization, leaving task structure, geometric relations, and constraints implicit. We present V2-STRep, a zero-shot framework that converts generated video motion into reusable robot skills through VLM-grounded structured task representations.

The representation specifies motion phases, references, and task-relevant constraints, with targets described by minimal geometric structures: points, point-normals, axes, planes, and full 6D poses. VLM-provided 2D image-space cues are lifted into 3D using RGB-D observations to reconstruct task geometry and candidate grasp poses.

Geometry-specific rules transfer motion to new scenes, while task-constrained trajectory optimization couples grasp selection with complete robot motion planning. It preserves task requirements while using remaining rotational freedom to accommodate joint limits.

Updating deployment grounding and constraints enables reuse under new compatible instructions without generating another video. Experiments on six real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improved execution success over baselines, reliable cross-scene transfer of successfully acquired skills, and adaptation to changed deployment instructions.

Details are available on the project website: https://tuwien-asl.github.io/V2-STRep/.

summary.en: The paper presents V2-STRep, a zero-shot framework for turning motion in generated videos into reusable robot skills. It combines vision-language-model image cues with RGB-D observations to reconstruct task geometry, candidate grasps, motion phases, and constraints. Geometry-specific rules and trajectory optimization support transfer to new scenes and instructions. Experiments on six real-world manipulation tasks reportedly show higher execution success than baselines, as well as cross-scene transfer and adaptation to changed deployment instructions.

Real robot data, rich across tasks and morphologies, is often treated as the bottleneck for training robot learning models, including embodied foundation models that aim for zero-shot physical transfer. In this paper, we investigate the degree to which such models can acquire necessary structure using data from systems without embodiment.

To this end, we test if inexpensive, procedurally generated synthetic data can yield useful priors before a model observes any real-world behavior. We study this through robot action prediction, a natural pretraining objective and a direct test of whether structure learned from arbitrary synthetic tasks transfers to embodied settings.

We introduce three data generation pipelines that model mathematical abstractions of robotic control, and use them as pretraining priors for a Transformer.

We demonstrate that a model trained purely on this non-robotic data attains non-trivial zero-shot prediction performance on unseen physical robot tasks via an in-context learning mechanism, and that our specialized control priors notably improve upon generic causal priors.

We also compare against a compute-matched baseline trained on real robot data, and find that it outperforms our model but only on the datasets it was trained on. These findings suggest that procedurally generated, mathematical abstractions can yield useful robotic priors, offering a potential complement to expensive embodied data collection.

summary.en: The paper investigates whether synthetic data from systems without embodiment can provide useful priors for robot learning. It introduces three pipelines that generate data from mathematical abstractions of robotic control and uses them to pretrain a Transformer. A model trained only on this data achieves non-trivial zero-shot prediction on unseen physical robot tasks through in-context learning; specialized control priors outperform generic causal priors. A compute-matched model trained on real robot data performs better, but only on datasets included in its training.

sections.text:
Natural-language interfaces allow users to command robotic systems without interacting directly with mission planners or robotics middleware. Their reliable use depends on robot tool routing, defined here as the selection of the smallest complete subset of predefined executable capabilities required to satisfy a request.

This task is particularly difficult for compound instructions, where incomplete selection may omit necessary sensing or monitoring capabilities, while excessive selection may expose irrelevant tools.

We compare four routing strategies: three progressively refined ChromaDB-based methods - fixed-threshold retrieval, relative-distance retrieval, and clause-aware aggregated retrieval - and a cloud-hosted 120-billion-parameter language-model baseline.

The methods are evaluated on 164 manually annotated prompts organised into three complexity levels, from direct single-tool requests to compound requests requiring at least three tools.

Using exact-match accuracy, completeness, precision, a completeness-weighted composite score, and routing latency, CDB-v3 achieves the best macro-average score among the retrieval-only methods, with 0.7822, compared with 0.8869 for the large-model baseline.

Although the LLM provides higher routing quality, CDB-v3 exhibits substantially lower latency and can be deployed locally without requiring cloud connectivity.

These results identify a quality-latency trade-off between direct large-model selection and clause-aware semantic retrieval for privacy-sensitive, connectivity-constrained, and resource-constrained robotic systems.

summary.en: The paper compares four strategies for routing natural-language robot requests to executable tools: three progressively refined ChromaDB retrieval methods and a cloud-hosted large language model. Evaluation uses 164 manually annotated prompts of varying complexity and measures exact-match accuracy, completeness, precision, a composite score, and latency. CDB-v3 has the best macro-average score among retrieval methods at 0.7822, while the model scores 0.8869 and provides higher routing quality. CDB-v3 has substantially lower latency and supports local deployment without cloud connectivity.

sections.text:
This chapter explores how robotic systems and ambient intelligence can enhance care for older adults in residential aged care (RAC) homes and private homes.

Although these settings differ, we frame both as extreme and challenging environments for human-robot interaction (HRI), characterised by cluttered and dynamic layouts, diverse resident needs, and limited on-site technical support.

We review embodied and non-embodied systems that assist with daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, highlighting hybrid deployments where robots complement fixed and wearable sensors. To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults.

Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers.

Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation.

Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.

summary.en: This chapter examines how robotic systems and ambient intelligence may support older adults in residential care and private homes, which it frames as challenging HRI environments. It reviews embodied and non-embodied systems for daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, including deployments alongside fixed and wearable sensors. The authors discuss accessible interaction, privacy, trust, and acceptability, and recommend real-world evaluation measures such as false alarms, fault recovery time, staff workload, and long-term reliability. They outline research directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments.
summary.zh: 本章讨论机器人系统与环境智能如何辅助养老机构和私人住宅中的老年人照护，并将两类场所都视为人机交互面临的复杂环境，特点包括布局杂乱且动态、居民需求多样和现场技术支持有限。作者回顾用于日常生活、安全监测和社交参与的具身及非具身系统，以及机器人与固定、可穿戴传感器的组合部署。设计建议关注老年人的认知、身体和社交需求，并强调易用交互、隐私、信任和可接受性。评估应关注真实环境指标，如误报、故障恢复时间、员工工作量和长期可靠性；章节还提出可扩展、符合监管要求的部署研究方向。

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack.

We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions.

To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150-episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria.

Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^-4).Crucially, excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00).

This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently.

The performance gap is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.

summary.en: Alpha is a framework for injecting faults and evaluating robustness in simulated LLM-driven manipulation. It covers perception lag, grip slip, unreachable targets, and corrupted planner output. The authors compare an LLM agent with a deterministic scripted planner under matched seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. In the reported episode matrix, the oracle performs better overall; when planner-output corruption is excluded, both achieve identical performance across physical and kinematic conditions. The authors attribute the overall gap to the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface, within this simulation evaluation.

Capturing a loose object inside a spacecraft requires a robot to approach a target that can translate and rotate, and whose motion changes when contact is made. These conditions motivate evaluation beyond manipulation of supported objects.

We introduce AstroBench, an open benchmark for free-floating capture and space robotic manipulation with a fixed-base arm. The task suite combines four initial-motion tracks with sample-storage operations based on MELFI hardware and cap and captive-screw servicing based on the Robotic Refueling Mission.

The two workcells provide nine task definitions and 29 task-target combinations. A metadata-filtered Objaverse inventory supplies 8,414 object instances for asset expansion, alongside five cabin visual contexts and versioned task instructions. We report two acquisition-focused experiments using existing checkpoints.

A frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ DROID joint-position policy captures 2 of 200 static targets and 4 of 200 moving targets across twenty object identities. A cube-specific ACT policy captures 8 of 10 static targets and 6 of 10 moving targets in a separate experiment. Each experiment retains its recorded observation, action and capture configuration.

The results document difficult direct transfer for the tested generalist checkpoint and successful task-specific capture behavior, while identifying concrete settings for studying motion-aware perception and contact-sensitive control. Code, task definitions and editable workcell assets are available at https://github.com/AstroUpLab/AstroBench.

summary.en: The paper introduces AstroBench, an open benchmark for free-floating object capture and space manipulation with a fixed-base arm. Its suite includes four initial-motion tracks, sample storage, and cap and captive-screw servicing, organized into two workcells and nine task definitions. The authors report two acquisition experiments with existing checkpoints: a generalist policy captured few targets, while a cube-specific policy showed task-specific capture behavior in a separate experiment.

Generated robot videos can look convincing while depicting the wrong interac- tion: a different object is moved, a grasp disappears, or a placement ends out- side its destination. We introduce RGraph-Eval, a reference-based framework that makes these discrepancies explicit through task-grounded temporal scene graphs.

Unlike approaches that construct separate evidence representations for different evaluation dimensions, we organize task entities, interactions, and motion within a unified, interpretable scene graph representation.

A foundation-model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, grounds persistent object masks, infers and verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs manipulated- object motion in three dimensions.

Applying this representation to a generated video and a reference demonstration supports an interpretable RGraph-Eval score with visible-object, relation-change, and 3D path-shape components. We also introduce ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources annotated with the multimodal representation.

Our eval- uation separates graph-generation quality from agreement with human video judgments, and includes comparisons with adapted SVG2 and SG-Ego, a bench- mark of three video generators.

The framework connects robot-video assessment to the observable entities and interactions underlying a task, while making the graph annotations reusable beyond evaluation. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/SashaDance/rgraph-eval.

Its unified representation organizes task entities, interactions, and motion. A foundation-model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, tracks object masks, verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs 3D motion. The resulting score has visible-object, relation-change, and 3D path-shape components. The authors also introduce ShareRobot-SG and report evaluations separating graph-generation quality from agreement with human judgments.

The assessment of planktonic standing stocks and microorganism structures is critical for understanding upper ocean biological processes.

Currently, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) equipped with in-situ optical imaging and artificial intelligence (AI) methods offer a promising solution for persistent surveillance, mapping and monitoring of planktonic life.

However, current AI methods often lack robustness in dynamic, unstructured environments, where environmental noise and non-biological artifacts lead to frequent misclassifications.

Standard convolutional neural network (CNN) classifiers often struggle with such conditions, leading to misclassifications that require time-consuming manual validation by marine biologists. To address this issue, we propose a novel robustness verification framework for in-situ plankton classifiers based on reachability analysis.

We also introduce a continuous-time neural ordinary differential equation (neural ODE) classification model leveraging the high-resolution imaging capabilities of the SilCam particle imager.

In this paper, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework by formally verifying the robustness of the neural ODE model against environmental perturbations.

We demonstrate that our verification framework acts as an automated filter providing formal guarantees of model stability against ambiguous data, thereby improving the reliability of autonomous sampling and reducing the post-processing workload.

summary.en: The paper proposes a reachability-analysis framework for verifying the robustness of plankton classifiers used on autonomous underwater vehicles, alongside a continuous-time neural ODE classifier that uses SilCam imaging. The authors report formally verifying the model against environmental perturbations. They describe the framework as an automated filter that provides formal guarantees of model stability for ambiguous data, with the stated aim of improving autonomous sampling reliability and reducing post-processing work.

Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone. Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force.

We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing. VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns. The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment.

The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4x4 array. We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments. In controlled single-taxel tests over 1-5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces.

A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use. Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact.

Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.

summary.en: The paper introduces VecTile, a thin, flexible tactile array that uses a piezoresistive layer and silicone nubs to turn normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns for three-axis force sensing. It can be fabricated without specialized equipment. The authors validate the sensing mechanism with finite element analysis and hardware experiments, and describe tests of curved use, brief manual calibration, scalpel contact with a balloon, and power-plug insertion.

sections.text:
We present OpenTac, a novel sensor and a full-stack ecosystem for tactile skins that are highly customizable, scalable, and readily deployed in downstream robot control and learning applications. Our core contribution is twofold.

First, we develop a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts tangential loading into spatially varying pressure. Differential responses across neighboring "taxels" support decoding of local shear vectors, and the common-mode response encodes normal force.

Second, we provide a highly customizable sensor design tool that is able to automatically generate fabrication files for these tactile skins from 2D outlines and developable 3D surfaces, including from abstract descriptions such as text (e.g., "design a sensor for a size 9 shoe insole").

We develop an ecosystem around the OpenTac sensor, including the CAD design tool, a sensor simulator, cross-sensor transfer, and fast/adaptive data acquisition. We demonstrate the broad applicability of the OpenTac-CAD sensor design tool by designing and fabricating more than 30 sensors across a variety of robot embodiments.

We characterize the three-dimensional tactile fields produced by OpenTac with a commercial, high-precision force/torque sensor. We demonstrate the broad applicability of 3D tactile sensing across contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning on four real-world robot embodiments.

Additionally, adaptive acquisition enables kilohertz-rate partial readouts, exceeding full-array raster scanning on the same sensor by 19.2X at 16 sampled taxels per update for a 1024-taxel skin. We provide all hardware, software, and result videos are at opentac.github.io

summary.en: The paper presents OpenTac, a customizable tactile skin and supporting ecosystem. A structured deformable overlay converts tangential loading into spatial pressure variation; differences between neighboring taxels encode local shear vectors, while common-mode response encodes normal force. The ecosystem includes a design tool that generates fabrication files from 2D outlines or developable 3D surfaces, plus simulation, cross-sensor transfer, and adaptive acquisition. The authors report sensor characterization and applications on real-world robot embodiments.

sections.text:
Swarm robotics relies on robots with minimal sensing and computation that achieve self-organization at the level of the collective to address a variety of tasks.

Yet swarm robotics still struggles with global tasks that require understanding the broader spatial context in which robots operate, such as identifying the shape of the arena in which they are embedded.

Here, we introduce spectral swarm robotics, a framework in which robots recover global spectral descriptors of the swarm's geometric structure through strictly local interactions. To do so, robots emulate diffusion to locally estimate Laplacian spectral invariants, quantities normally obtained only through centralized computation.

These spectral values serve as compact descriptors of the environment. In the present proof of concept, robots estimated the second Laplacian eigenvalue and used it to classify arenas from a predefined set of shapes with distinct spectral signatures.

We show that estimating a single eigenvalue is sufficient for one-shot classification among selected confined environments with distinct spectral signatures. We uncovered a scaling law linking swarm size (a global parameter) and interaction radius (a local parameter) that ensures robust estimation.

We validated the approach experimentally on two distinct hardware platforms, Kilobots and Pogobots, achieving reliable classification of arena shapes under realistic noise and sparse-connectivity conditions.

Last, we discuss how locally recovering Laplacian spectral invariants opens avenues for swarm robotics in settings where producing efficient collective behaviors strongly depends on the global structure of the swarm.

summary.en: The paper introduces spectral swarm robotics, in which robots use local interactions to emulate diffusion and estimate Laplacian spectral invariants of the swarm’s geometry. In a proof of concept, robots estimate the second Laplacian eigenvalue to classify arena shapes from a predefined set with distinct spectral signatures. The authors report a scaling law relating swarm size and interaction radius, and experiments on Kilobots and Pogobots showing reliable classification under noise and sparse connectivity.

items.title: Hearing the shape of an arena with spectral swarm robotics

sections.text:
Humanoid robots must coordinate locomotion and manipulation in everyday environments, yet progress is difficult to assess across differing policies, controllers, and task settings. LocoManiLab provides an integrated testbed spanning data collection and generation, policy training, evaluation, and physical deployment.

Its task suite covers 234 atomic and compositional tasks across five household scene categories, supported by 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation.

The evaluation covers twelve policies with a shared controller across task and scene splits and perturbation levels, two policies across five controllers, and studies of demonstration scale and data-source mixtures.

Success rates fall on unseen tasks and scenes and generally decline as visual perturbations increase, with differences in generalization and robustness across policies.

For data generation, a humanoid motion generation model is fine-tuned for loco-manipulation to study the alignment of its outputs with task execution requirements and its integration into the data generation pipeline. Three simulated loco-manipulation tasks closely match real-world setups, enabling evaluation of three policies in both domains.

Similar policy rankings support the reliability of simulation-based evaluation.

summary.en: The paper presents LocoManiLab, an integrated testbed for humanoid loco-manipulation covering data collection and generation, policy training, evaluation, and physical deployment. Its task suite spans household scenes and includes simulated teleoperation data. Evaluations compare policies and controllers across task and scene splits, visual perturbations, demonstration scales, and data-source mixtures. Success rates decline on unseen tasks and scenes and generally decrease with stronger visual perturbations. The authors also study motion-model fine-tuning and report similar policy rankings in simulation and real-world setups as evidence for simulation-based evaluation.
summary.zh: 论文提出 LocoManiLab，这是用于人形机器人移动操作的综合测试平台，覆盖数据采集与生成、策略训练、评估和实体部署。任务集包含五类家庭场景中的原子及组合任务，并使用模拟遥操作数据。评估比较了多种策略和控制器，考察任务与场景迁移、视觉扰动、演示规模及数据来源混合。结果显示，未见任务和场景上的成功率下降，视觉扰动增强时成功率通常也下降。研究还将运动生成模型微调用于移动操作，并比较模拟与现实设置中的策略表现；相近的策略排名被作者视为支持模拟评估可靠性的证据。

sections.text:
Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to constraints over groups of robots.

Existing methods that approach joint optimality remain largely centralized, offline, and confined to collision-free motion planning, while decentralized, real-time counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process.

We extend a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of forward-propagated commands for differentially flat systems to coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement.

It is this structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the search of each robot's tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence.

Our protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short.

In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37% against a decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity.

Hardware experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world implementability.

summary.en: The paper introduces WarpWeaver, a decentralized real-time planner for coordinating nonlinear multi-robot systems toward a joint optimum over a receding horizon. It extends a single-robot dispersive-tree framework and coordinates search through asynchronous negotiation over shared-space constraints. The authors state that near-optimality can be certified when negotiation reaches quiescence. In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time relative to centralized offline planners and a decentralized real-time baseline, and improves success on a graph-connectivity task. Onboard planning experiments with six robots demonstrate implementability in hardware.
summary.zh: 论文提出 WarpWeaver，一种面向非线性多机器人系统的分散式实时规划器，目标是在滚动时域中逐步接近联合最优。方法扩展了基于前向传播命令离散树的单机器人框架，并通过异步协商共享空间约束来协调各机器人的搜索；协商静止时可认证协议所得方案的近优性。作者报告，仿真中该方法相较集中式离线规划器和分散式实时基线降低总行程时间，并提高图连通任务的成功率。六台机器人机载规划的硬件实验展示了现实环境中的可实施性。

sections.text:
We consider the offline generation of coordinated paths for N interchangeable robots and N goals in planar environments with polygonal obstacles.

After a conformal map to a circular domain, starts and goals become the poles and zeros of a rational function R, and the paths are the branches of its Generalized Root Locus (GRL), i.e. the streamlines of the logarithmic potential -log R.

We show that, for every phase outside a finite set of critical phases and a set of boundary phases, the induced gradient motion drives each robot to a distinct goal along pairwise disjoint paths that never reach the obstacles; the robot-goal assignment is produced by the construction, and with the gain used as a clock all robots move as the closed-loop roots of the GRL and arrive together at a prescribed time.

Obstacles become streamlines through successive Milne-Thomson reflections, and for a finite number of reflections a finite test certifies safety for the potential that is actually computed. Reciprocal root-locus planning is recovered as a special case.

The method is illustrated on two polygonal workspaces, 100 random instances compared with independent harmonic planning and artificial potentials, and a scene with ten robots and ten obstacles.

summary.en: The paper studies offline coordinated path generation for interchangeable robots and goals in planar environments with polygonal obstacles. After mapping the environment to a circular domain, it represents starts and goals as poles and zeros of a rational function and generates paths using its Generalized Root Locus. The authors show that, for phases outside specified finite exceptional sets, robots reach distinct goals along disjoint paths that avoid obstacles and can arrive together at a prescribed time. Obstacles are handled through successive Milne-Thomson reflections, with a finite safety test for the computed potential when reflections are finite. Examples include polygonal workspaces and random instances.

sections.text:
Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time.

However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated.

Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object.

We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating.

Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points.

Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated.

Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.

summary.en: The authors propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that updates confidence for individual object points using multi-view temporal evidence. Consistent observations reinforce points, while inconsistent segmentation, depth, and visibility cues reduce confidence in noisy or obsolete points. Object tracking and re-identification help preserve identities through motion and relocation. Experiments report better mapping accuracy than a previous method on Replica and ScanNet, robustness to dynamic scenes and perception noise, and success rates for object navigation and embodied question answering.
summary.zh: 本文提出一种在线可精炼语义映射框架，通过多视角时序证据更新对象点的置信度，以强化可靠点并抑制由分割、深度或可见性误差造成的噪声和过时点；结合跟踪与重识别维持物体移动或重定位后的实例身份。作者报告，该方法在Replica和ScanNet上的映射准确率优于先前方法，并在动态环境和感知噪声下表现稳健；导航和具身问答成功率分别为82.4%和76.7%。

sections.text:
Agentic robot systems combine language-model reasoning with robot policies to monitor execution and recover from failures. However, reviewing every action chunk incurs substantial overhead, even in familiar situations. We introduce FastHarness, an experience-driven execution harness that adaptively schedules GPT-6 Astra supervision of a {\pi}0.5 policy.

A fast path uses stage memory and reviewed outcomes to reduce review frequency as experience accumulates, while a complementary recovery path focuses supervision on correcting errors. Once recovery is verified, routine execution resumes, with failure experience retained to guide future interventions.

The policy remains frozen and generates fresh actions from current observations. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use decreases by an average of 57.2% per task from the first evaluated episode to the mean of the final five episodes. Mean episode time decreases from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes over the same interval.

On the same tasks, mean success increases from 80% for GPT-as-Policy ({\pi}0.5 + GPT-6 Astra) to 97.19% with FastHarness. These results highlight adaptive supervision as a practical route to more efficient agentic robotics without additional model training.

summary.en: FastHarness is an experience-driven execution harness that adaptively schedules GPT-6 Astra supervision for a frozen π0.5 policy. A fast path reduces review frequency as experience accumulates, while a recovery path directs supervision toward errors and returns to routine execution after recovery is verified. In four simulated manipulation tasks, reviewer token use per task fell by an average of 57.2% from the first evaluated episode to the final-five-episode mean, and mean episode time decreased from 85.5 to 52.0 minutes. Mean success rose from 80% to 97.19%.

sections.text:
Motion planning is central to robotics, and it is increasingly used to correct the motions proposed by learned planners and policies. In both uses, constraints must hold at every instant of the motion, not only at sampled times.

To our knowledge, no algorithm provably converges to a globally optimal motion once a smoothness cost is combined with such constraints. We cast planning and steering as a single continuous-time program: robots avoid one another and static or moving obstacles, and a learned proposal is steered by keeping the motion close to it.

The program is elementary to state, yet nonconvex. We propose GlobMP (Global Motion Planning), a gradient projection method over piecewise-polynomial curves, on which each constraint is one polynomial per piece that must stay nonnegative over the whole motion; it alternates cost reduction with feasibility restoration.

Under mild assumptions, we show that, from a fine grid start, its cost approaches the global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces grows, with every constraint met to any chosen tolerance, or exactly on stable instances.

We demonstrate its superior performance over strong baselines in real and synthetic experiments, including teams of up to $200$ robots, multi-robot planning on the Robotarium testbed and an extended benchmark, maze navigation, and steering tactile-reactive policies on a bimanual humanoid.

summary.en: The paper formulates motion planning and steering as a continuous-time program, enforcing obstacle avoidance throughout the motion and keeping steered trajectories close to learned proposals. GlobMP applies gradient projection to piecewise-polynomial curves, alternating cost reduction with feasibility restoration. Under mild assumptions and from a sufficiently fine-grid start, the authors show that cost approaches the global optimum as the number of pieces grows, while constraints meet a chosen tolerance or are exact on stable instances. Real and synthetic experiments include multi-robot planning, maze navigation, and policy steering.
summary.zh: 本文将运动规划与转向表述为连续时间优化问题，要求机器人在整个运动过程中避开彼此及静态或移动障碍，并使转向后的运动接近学习型规划器提出的轨迹。作者提出GlobMP，在分段多项式曲线上使用梯度投影，交替降低代价与恢复可行性。理论结果表明，在温和假设下，从足够细的网格初始化时，随着多项式片段数增加，代价趋近全局最优，约束可达到任意指定容差，稳定情形下可精确满足。实验涵盖真实与合成场景及多机器人任务。

sections.text:
In recent human-robot collaboration environments, there is a growing focus on integrating diverse sensor data beyond visual information to enable safer and more intelligent task execution. Although thermal data can be crucial for enhancing robot safety and operational efficiency, its integration has been relatively overlooked in prior research.

This paper proposes a novel Vision-Language-Action (VLA) framework that incorporates thermal information for robot task execution. The proposed system leverages a Vision-Language Model (VLM) as a high-level planner to interpret complex natural language commands and decompose them into simpler sub-tasks.

This approach facilitates efficient data collection and robust reasoning for complex operations. Unlike conventional methods that rely solely on visual data, our approach integrates thermal information, enabling the robot to perceive physical properties and proactively ensure environmental safety.

Experimental results from real-world task scenarios validate the feasibility of our proposed framework, suggesting its potential to enhance task success rates and safety compared to existing vision-based systems.Project page: https://youngchae912.github.io/ThermoAct/

summary.en: The paper presents ThermoAct, a vision-language-action framework that incorporates thermal information into robot task execution. A vision-language model acts as a high-level planner, interpreting natural-language commands and decomposing them into subtasks. Thermal input is used to perceive physical properties and proactively support environmental safety. The authors report that experiments in real-world task scenarios validate feasibility and suggest potential improvements in task success and safety compared with existing vision-based systems.

Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control.

World-model-based reinforcement learning provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot's own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency.

We propose DiffDreamer, a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization.

In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot's explicit physical state.

We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards.

Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods.

Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.

summary.en: DiffDreamer couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation to optimize an actor for quadrotor control. The world model propagates latent states for external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the simulator propagates the robot’s explicit physical state. The actor objective separates a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards from a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments in aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing report improved convergence and final performance over several baselines; the paper also describes ablations and proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments.

sections.text:
Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control.

We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model. We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation.

These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program.

We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences.

Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output.

Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.

summary.en: PhysibleMDM improves the physical feasibility of motion diffusion outputs by optimizing diffusion noise at inference time, without retraining the generative model. It combines kinematic checks for ground penetration, slip, and self-collision with dynamic feasibility tests based on an inverse-dynamics cone-program inner loop. Sep-CMA-ES solves the black-box optimization, and an autoregressive scheme chains optimized segments. The authors report reductions in several penetration, slip, acceleration-reconstruction, and inverse-dynamics error measures across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid and 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot.

sections.text:
Robot demonstrations record what the robot saw and what it did. They do not specify how the 3D world changed in between. Scene-level 3D flow describes it by tracking 3D scene points, providing the world representation with 4D geometry. Prior work has used flow to improve robot policies.

Flow served as an intermediate prediction that a separate model converts into actions, as a prior injected at inference time, or as an extra output learned together with the action. In all of these designs, flow stays outside the policy, as a separate module or as an extra prediction head.

We introduce UniFlowWAM, a Unified World-Action Model that makes 3D scene flow a third modality on par with vision and action. Its world representation therefore covers both visual semantics, through future visual features, and 4D geometry, through 3D flow, and flow receives its own supervision.

UniFlowWAM is a diffusion transformer with one expert per modality, and the three experts exchange information through joint attention. We train UniFlowWAM under a ten-objective role grid, where each objective assigns every modality exactly one of three roles, namely target, condition, or absent.

The same model thus serves as a policy, as forward and inverse dynamics, and as a predictor of future visual features or 3D flow. We evaluate UniFlowWAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus in simulation, and on four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks.

On RoboCasa-GR1, UniFlowWAM raises the success rate of its base model without flow from 52.1% to 56.4%.It preserves in-distribution success on LIBERO at 98.1% and reaches 87.7% zero-shot on LIBERO-Plus. On the real robot, it achieves 87.0% average success, compared with 68.5% for the strongest baseline.

summary.en: UniFlowWAM treats 3D scene flow as a third modality alongside vision and action, with modality-specific experts exchanging information through joint attention. Its world representation combines visual semantics from future visual features with 4D geometry from 3D flow. The same model supports policy learning, forward and inverse dynamics, and prediction of future visual features or flow. Evaluation includes simulation benchmarks RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, plus four real-world bimanual manipulation tasks; the authors report success-rate results across these settings.
summary.zh: 论文提出 UniFlowWAM，将三维场景流作为与视觉、动作并列的第三种模态，并通过联合注意力连接各模态专家。其世界表征同时涵盖未来视觉特征所表达的语义和三维流所表达的四维几何；同一模型可用于策略、正向与逆向动力学，以及未来特征或场景流预测。仿真评估覆盖 RoboCasa-GR1、LIBERO 和 LIBERO-Plus，另有四项真实世界双臂操作任务。作者报告了各基准和真实机器人上的成功率结果。

sections.text:
Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions.

However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored.

We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions.

Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties.

To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction.

Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.

summary.en: Echo is a framework for learning task status and generating actions within a single vision-language-action model. It represents status with stop and failure signals added as two dimensions of each action chunk, and denoises them together with robot actions to distinguish ongoing execution, success, and failure. The method uses successful, failed, and recovery trajectories without frame-level progress annotations. The authors report that real-world manipulation experiments show accurate status prediction and consistent policy performance improvements.
summary.zh: Echo 面向视觉语言动作模型中的任务状态识别与动作生成。它将停止和失败信号作为动作块的两个维度，与机器人动作一起去噪，以区分任务进行中、成功完成和失败。框架通过成功、失败及恢复轨迹学习状态信号，不依赖逐帧进度标注；并控制信号与动作的交互，使信号比动作更快去噪。作者报告，真实世界操作实验显示 Echo 能准确预测任务状态，并持续提升策略表现。

items.title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models

sections.text:
Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions. Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal. However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history.

We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed. We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE.

Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches. Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history.

We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution. Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.

summary.en: NavBind diagnoses whether navigation vision-language-action models bind instructions to actions. It holds the navigation context fixed, changes instructions at route forks, and compares generated local action sequences, the likelihood of fixed reference sequences under each instruction, and changes in visual attention and attribution. The study constructs 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE. Across evaluated models, the authors report that higher navigation success does not imply more faithful instruction following.

Deformable granular terrains introduce significant locomotion and immobilization risks in planetary exploration and are difficult to detect via remote sensing (e.g., vision).Legged robots can sense terrain properties through leg-terrain interactions during locomotion, offering a direct means to assess traversability in deformable environments.

How to systematically exploit this interaction-derived information for navigation planning, however, remains underexplored. We address this gap by presenting PSANE, a Proprioceptive Safe Active Navigation and Exploration framework that leverages leg-terrain interaction measurements for safe navigation and exploration in unknown deformable environments.

PSANE learns a traversability model via Gaussian Process regression to estimate and certify safe regions and identify exploration frontiers online, and integrates these estimates with a reactive controller for real-time navigation.

Frontier selection is formulated as a multi-objective optimization that balances safe-set expansion probability and goal-directed cost, with subgoals selected via scalarization over the Pareto-optimal frontier set.

PSANE safely explores unknown granular terrain and reaches specified goals using only proprioceptively estimated traversability, while achieving performance improvements over baseline methods.

summary.en: PSANE is a safe active navigation and exploration framework for unknown deformable terrain. It uses measurements from leg-terrain interactions to estimate traversability, learning a model with Gaussian Process regression to identify and certify safe regions and discover exploration frontiers online. A reactive controller uses these estimates for real-time navigation. Frontier selection balances the probability of expanding the safe set against goal-directed cost. The authors report that PSANE safely explores unknown granular terrain and reaches specified goals using proprioceptively estimated traversability, with performance improvements over baseline methods.
summary.zh: PSANE 是面向未知可变形地形的安全主动导航与探索框架，利用腿足与地形交互测量估计可通行性。它通过高斯过程回归学习可通行性模型，在线估计并认证安全区域、识别探索前沿，再将这些估计用于实时反应式控制。前沿选择采用多目标优化，权衡安全区域扩展概率和目标导向代价，并从帕累托最优前沿集合中选取子目标。作者报告，PSANE 仅凭本体感知估计的可通行性即可安全探索未知颗粒地形并到达指定目标，且表现优于基线方法。
